newsitem.title: CHINA: Warm reception seen for China Eastern listing.
newsitem.headline: Warm reception seen for China Eastern listing.

text.p: Foreign investors will be keen to buy shares of China Eastern, the first Chinese airline to be listed overseas, because of a rapidly growing market in which prices are highly regulated, brokers said on Thursday.
China Eastern Airlines (CEA) will list in New York and Hong Kong simultaneously at the beginning of 1997, to be followed by China Southern Airlines, Xinhua news agency said on Wednesday.

It gave no details of the date, price or size of the listing. CEA officials on Thursday declined comment, saying that the company's lawyers did not allow them to say anything about the listing because of legal restrictions in the United States.
"There is tremendous demand for travel and more and more inter-regional trade in China," said John Crossman, general manager of Jardine Fleming Securities in Shanghai.
"China will never get a highway system as in the United States. If you want to do business and inter-regional trade, you have to go by air," he said.

Shanghai and Guangzhou, base of China Southern, are the two best hubs in China as the centre of large business regions, he said. "If you believe Shanghai will develop as a financial and business centre, this (CEA) is a good proxy."
A Chinese broker said the country's tightly regulated airline market was a plus for airlines and investors.
Beijing sets prices and there is no likelihood of U.S.-style price wars in the foreseeable future, he said.

The aviation market is growing at 20 percent a year from a low base, he said. "There is big potential, especially for an airline based in Shanghai. Many investors will want to buy CEA shares. The concept is very good."

CEA's annual report for 1995 said that it posted unaudited net profit of 500 million yuan ($60.2 million) on a turnover of seven billion yuan, with a fleet of 39 McDonnell Douglas, Airbus and Fokker planes flying 88 domestic and 23 foreign routes. It gave no comparative 1994 figures.
The airline accounted for 14.38 percent of the total turnover of China's airlines in 1995, the report said.
A second Chinese broker said CEA made the correct decision in shifting to a dual Hong Kong-New York listing from its original plan to list only in New York.

"China funds are based in Hong Kong, so it makes more sense to list them," he said. "The New York listing is necessary because many U.S. funds have legal restrictions on buying shares outside the U.S."

But CEA may not be the first Chinese airline to list public shares. Hainan Airlines, a joint venture based in the southern island of Hainan, has been given approval to list foreign currency B shares in Shanghai.
An official of Hainan Airlines said on Thursday the company planned to issue 71 million B shares in the first quarter of 1997 in Shanghai. He gave no more details.

Hainan Airlines is 25 percent owned by American Aviation Investment, a fund partially controlled by U.S. financier George Soros, and is the first China airline to become a joint venture company. ($1=8.3 yuan)
